intro: A standard outdoor track is 400 meters in the inside lane. Staggers make outer lanes fair. A stopwatch and later a photo-finish camera turn a race into a record. The IHSA lists track and field champions from 1893.

Many U.S. school pools are 25 yards. Olympic pools are 50 meters. Wingfield patented a lawn-tennis kit in 1873. Wimbledon began in 1877. IHSA boys swimming is listed at 1932, girls swimming at 1975, boys tennis at 1912, and girls tennis at 1972.
bigQuestion: How did clocks, ropes, and painted lines make races and games comparable across towns?

chapters.title: A Clock on a Track
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a running race become eight lanes and eight times?

story.title: A Hand Drops
story.kicker: A hand drops and eight lanes become eight times.
paragraphs: Eight painted lanes curve around an oval. A starter holds a gun or a whistle. When the signal comes, eight bodies become eight times. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
A standard outdoor track is 400 meters around in the inside lane. World Athletics writes many of those technical rules. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
Time is an object here: a stopwatch, later a photo-finish camera. The clock is as much a part of the room as the paint. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
The IHSA crowned its first track and field state champions in 1893, earlier than most of its other sport series. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
story.think: What does a stopwatch remember that the dirt will forget?

lessons.title: Four Hundred Meters
lessons.mainIdea: A standard outdoor running track is 400 meters around in the inside lane.
reading: World Athletics sets the standard outdoor lap at 400 meters in lane one. School tracks in many countries copy that length.
Older American meets used yards. A 440-yard lap is close to 400 meters but is not the same number.
When two schools compare times, they need to know which lap they ran.

words.d: one full trip around the track
the international body that writes many track technical rules

lessons.title: Lanes as Fair Paper
lessons.mainIdea: Staggered starting marks make the outer lanes as long as the inside lane for one lap.
reading: An outer lane is a bigger circle. If every runner started on the same line, the outside runner would run farther.
Staggered starts paint a different mark in each lane so one full lap is the same distance.
The stagger is geometry on the ground. It is a fairness tool written into the marks.

words.d: a marked strip one runner stays in
a starting mark moved forward in outer lanes

look.text: Look at eight starting marks that step forward as the lanes go out. The finish line is one painted bar.
look.prompt: Why don't the outer-lane marks sit even with lane one?

choices: one lap is the same distance

lessons.title: The Ancient Stadium
lessons.mainIdea: The ancient Olympic Games at Olympia included a sprint in a stadium, a long dirt path.
reading: A stade was a unit of length and a place. Runners raced a straight path, not a modern 400-meter oval.
The traditional date for the first ancient Olympic Games is 776 BCE. That date is a later count, not a stopwatch tape.
Modern ovals and ancient paths are both rooms built so a race can be seen.

words.d: the place in Greece of the ancient Olympic Games
an ancient race path and a unit of length

lessons.title: The Stopwatch
lessons.mainIdea: A stopwatch turns a race into a number a page can keep.
reading: Before pocket watches were common, races were won by the eye: who reached the mark first.
A stopwatch lets officials write minutes and seconds. Two meets on two days can be compared.
The object on the table is the watch, not a runner's stride.

words.d: a clock that starts and stops to measure a race
the person who writes the time as the meet record

lessons.title: Photo Finish
lessons.mainIdea: Photo-finish cameras later decided close races the eye could not split.
reading: At the tape, two runners can look even. A camera aimed at the finish line records the order.
Photo finish became standard in high-level meets in the twentieth century.
The picture is evidence. It is another kind of paper, made of light.

lessons.title: Starting Blocks
lessons.mainIdea: Starting blocks are a later tool that holds a sprinter's feet at the start.
reading: Older sprinters dug holes in the cinders for their feet. Blocks later gave a standard object.
World Athletics events use blocks in short races. The object belongs at the starting mark.
Blocks are gear. They are not a lesson in how to sprint.

words.d: a frame that holds a sprinter's feet at the start
the old burned-surface tracks where runners dug footholds

look.title: From holes to frames
look.text: Sprinters once dug footholds in cinder tracks. Starting blocks became the standard object at the start of short races.

lessons.title: IHSA Track, 1893
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA crowned its first track and field state champions in 1893.
reading: Among IHSA sports, track and field is early. The first champions were named in 1893, seven years before the association's 1900 founding date as now counted, in the lineage of Illinois school meets.
The IHSA history page lists Track and Field at 1893 for the first state champion.
School tracks in Illinois still host that series. The oval is a civic room like the gym.

lessons.title: A School Meet Needs Officials
lessons.mainIdea: A track meet needs starters, timers, and judges as well as runners.
reading: Someone must fire or blow the start. Someone must watch the line. Someone must write the time.
Those jobs are public. A meet without paper is only a practice.
IHSA series rules name how those officials work. The names of the jobs are history of the room.

words.d: the official who gives the start signal
the official who records the time

lessons.title: Comparing Marks Across Towns
lessons.mainIdea: Written times let a school in Cairo and a school in Rockford compare marks.
reading: If both run 400 meters on a marked track, the numbers can sit on one list.
If one school still ran yards and the other ran meters, the list would lie.
Shared length plus shared timing is why track paper travels.

chapters.title: Pool Length and a Tennis Line
chapters.bigQuestion: How did swimming and tennis become rooms people can measure?

story.title: A Rope on the Water
story.kicker: A rope floats across water to mark a length.
paragraphs: A lane rope floats on a pool. It does not keep anyone dry. It marks a path and a length. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
Many United States school pools are 25 yards long. An Olympic pool is 50 meters long. Times cannot mix those two lengths without a note. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
Tennis is a different measured room: a rectangle split by a net. The All England Club played its first Wimbledon in 1877. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
The IHSA lists boys swimming from 1932, girls swimming from 1975, boys tennis from 1912, and girls tennis from 1972. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
story.think: What do a floating rope and a painted tennis line both do?

lessons.title: Twenty-Five Yards and Fifty Meters
lessons.mainIdea: Many U.S. school pools are 25 yards. Olympic pools are 50 meters.
reading: Short-course yards is a common U.S. school and club length. Long-course meters is the Olympic length.
A time in a 25-yard pool is not the same as a time in a 50-meter pool. Record lists have to say which course.
World Aquatics, once called FINA, writes many world swimming rules.

words.d: a 25-yard or 25-meter pool
the world swimming body, formerly FINA

lessons.title: Lane Ropes
lessons.mainIdea: Floating lane ropes mark swimming paths and cut the splash between swimmers.
reading: A rope with floats sits on the water. It shows where one swimmer's path ends.
Ropes also calm waves between lanes. The object is part of the room.
Without ropes, a six-lane meet would be six arguments about space.

words.d: a floating line that marks a swimming lane
the beads that keep the rope on the surface

look.title: A rope that is not a rescue line
look.text: Look at a line of plastic floats from wall to wall. No one is climbing it. It is a border.
look.prompt: What argument does the rope stop?

lessons.title: IHSA Swimming Dates
lessons.mainIdea: IHSA boys swimming crowned a first champion in 1932. Girls swimming crowned a first champion in 1975.
reading: Boys swimming and diving is listed at 1932 on the IHSA history page. Girls swimming and diving is listed at 1975.
Those are school series dates. People swam in Illinois waters long before either year.
School pools, like gyms, are buildings a district heats and fills.

words.d: the Illinois High School Association
the board events paired with swimming in many school series

lessons.title: Wingfield and 1873
lessons.mainIdea: Major Walter Clopton Wingfield patented a lawn game in 1873 that helped launch modern tennis.
reading: Wingfield sold a boxed game called Sphairistikè. It used a net and a hourglass-like court on lawns.
The game spread in Britain and then abroad. The court later became a clear rectangle.
1873 is a patent-and-kit date, not the first time anyone hit a ball over a rope.

words.d: the British officer who patented a lawn-tennis kit in 1873
the name Wingfield used for his boxed lawn game

lessons.title: Wimbledon, 1877
lessons.mainIdea: The All England Club held its first Wimbledon tournament in 1877.
reading: The first Wimbledon was a gentlemen's singles event on grass. Spencer Gore won.
Wimbledon became tennis's most famous lawn meet. The club still plays on grass.
1877 is a tournament date. 1873 is the kit date. Keep both.

words.d: the All England Club's tennis tournament, first held in 1877
the winner of the first Wimbledon in 1877

lessons.title: Lines a Server Can See
lessons.mainIdea: A tennis court is a measured rectangle with a net in the middle and service boxes painted on both sides.
reading: The net is the wall you can see through. The lines name where a serve must land.
Two players who have never met can still use those lines. Paint does the introducing.
School courts copy that idea at different sizes and surfaces.

lessons.title: IHSA Tennis Dates
lessons.mainIdea: IHSA boys tennis crowned a first champion in 1912. Girls tennis crowned a first champion in 1972.
reading: Boys tennis is an early IHSA series, listed at 1912. Girls tennis is listed at 1972, the same year as Title IX.
1972 on the IHSA page is a school-title year. Title IX is a federal law from the same calendar year. They are different papers.
School courts, like pools, sit on district ground.

lessons.title: Two Rooms, One Idea
lessons.mainIdea: Pools and tennis courts both work because people agreed on a measured drawing.
reading: A pool length is a number. A tennis court is a number. Without the number, a record list cannot travel.
Track already taught that lesson with 400 meters. Water and court repeat it in other rooms.
The drawings differ. The idea does not: mark the room, write the mark.

lessons.title: Who Fills the Pool
lessons.mainIdea: A school pool is a tank a district fills, heats, and staffs.
reading: Water is heavy. Heat is expensive. Lifeguards are staff. A pool is one of the costliest civic sport rooms.
That is why many districts share a pool or rent a park-district tank.
Naming the cost keeps the pool in the civic family with the gym and the lighted field.

words.d: the trained staff who watch a pool
a local office that may own a pool schools rent
